books.title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
books.author: Cal Newport
books.description: Why "follow your passion" is bad career advice, and what works instead.
ideas: Passion follows mastery

"Follow your passion" sounds inspiring, but Cal Newport found that most people who love their work didn't start with a fully formed passion. They became passionate about work they'd become very good at, as skill brought respect, autonomy and meaning. Passion is often the result of mastery, not the starting point. Today: instead of asking "What's my passion?", ask "What could I get really good at, starting now?"
Career capital

Newport describes career capital: rare and valuable skills that you can trade for the things people want from work, like interesting projects, flexibility and impact. The more capital you build, the more control you gain over your career. Jumping to a dream job without capital rarely works. Today: identify one skill that's both rare and valuable in your field, and plan a small step to strengthen it this week.
The craftsman mindset

The craftsman mindset, Newport says, focuses on the value you can offer rather than what the job offers you. Instead of constantly asking whether your work is fulfilling enough, you ask how you can get better at it. Paradoxically, this mindset often leads to more fulfilment, because skill brings opportunities. Today: in your next task, focus entirely on doing it a little better than last time, and notice how that changes your experience.
Deliberate practice

Getting better at anything, Newport explains, requires deliberate practice: stretching beyond your comfort zone, with clear feedback. It's uncomfortable, like a musician practising the hardest passage over and over, rather than playing pieces they already know. Coasting at what you already do well builds no new capital. Today: choose one skill and spend twenty minutes practising the hardest part of it, with a way to measure progress.

books.title: Range
books.author: David Epstein
books.description: Why generalists often triumph in a world that celebrates early specialization.
ideas: Kind and wicked learning environments

Chess and golf have clear rules, quick feedback and repeated patterns. David Epstein calls them kind learning environments, where early specialisation works well. But most of life is wicked: rules are unclear, feedback is delayed and patterns change. In wicked environments, broad experience and flexible thinking often beat narrow expertise. Today: think about whether your work is more like chess or more like real life, and what that means for how you should learn.
The sampling period

Many top performers, Epstein found, tried many activities before settling on one. Roger Federer played several sports as a child before focusing on tennis. This sampling period helped them find a good match for their abilities and interests, which mattered more than starting early. Today: if you feel behind because you've changed paths, remember that exploring is often how people find the right fit.
Analogical thinking

People with broad experience can borrow solutions from unrelated fields. Epstein tells stories of outsiders who solved problems that insiders were stuck on, by drawing analogies from different domains: a chemist solving a biology puzzle, an engineer helping doctors. Breadth gives you more tools to think with. Today: take a problem you're facing and ask how someone from a completely different field might approach it.
Late starters aren't behind

Switching careers or starting late can feel like wasted time. Epstein argues the opposite: what you learned elsewhere often becomes an unusual advantage, a unique combination of skills and perspectives. Many successful people found their true path in their thirties, forties or later. Today: list three skills from past jobs or hobbies that could help you in your current goals.

books.title: Designing Your Life
books.author: Bill Burnett & Dave Evans
books.description: Two Stanford designers apply design thinking to building a career and life you love.
ideas: Prototype your career

Before making a big life change, Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, who teach design at Stanford, suggest building prototypes: small, cheap experiments that test the idea. Talk to people who already do the job, shadow someone for a day or take on a small project. You learn far more from trying than from imagining. Today: pick one career idea you're curious about and arrange a conversation with someone who already lives it.
Odyssey plans

The authors suggest an exercise called odyssey plans. Sketch three different versions of your next five years: one based on your current path, one for what you'd do if that path disappeared, and one for what you'd do if money and other people's opinions didn't matter. It loosens the feeling that there's only one right life. Today: spend twenty minutes sketching your three odyssey plans, and notice which one makes you feel most alive.
Gravity problems

Some problems, the authors say, are like gravity: you can't solve them, so struggling against them wastes energy. If a field pays poorly and you can't change that, it's a gravity problem. The useful move is to accept it and design around it: change your goals, find a niche or combine roles. Today: identify one gravity problem you've been fighting, and brainstorm ways to work with it instead.
Track your energy

For a few weeks, the authors suggest, keep a simple log of your daily activities and note how much energy and engagement each one gave or drained. Patterns emerge: maybe you light up in workshops but drain in long meetings. This good time journal reveals what kind of work fits you, often more accurately than personality tests. Today: start a simple log tonight, listing your activities and marking each with a plus or minus for energy.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
books.author: Stephen R. Covey
books.description: A principle-centred approach to personal and professional effectiveness.
ideas: Be proactive

Between what happens to us and how we respond, Stephen Covey wrote, there is a space, and in that space lies our freedom. Proactive people focus on what they can influence: their choices, attitudes and actions. Reactive people focus on what they can't control and blame circumstances. Being proactive doesn't mean being pushy; it means taking responsibility for your response. Today: when something frustrating happens, pause and ask, "What's within my control here?" Then act on that.
Begin with the end in mind

Covey suggests imagining your own funeral and hearing what family, friends and colleagues say about you. What would you want them to say? That picture reveals what truly matters to you. Beginning with the end in mind means letting that vision guide everyday choices, so you don't climb a ladder only to discover it's leaning against the wrong wall. Today: write a short description of the person you want to be remembered as, and choose one action that moves you toward it.
Put first things first

Covey sorted activities by urgency and importance. Urgent but unimportant tasks, like many emails and interruptions, eat our days. Important but not urgent ones, like planning, exercise, relationships and learning, are where real effectiveness lies, yet we often neglect them because nothing forces us to act. Today: schedule one important but not urgent activity this week and protect that time like an appointment.
Seek first to understand

Most people listen with the intent to reply, already preparing their answer while the other person is speaking. Covey encourages listening to understand first: trying to see the situation from the other person's perspective before sharing your own. People who feel understood are far more open to hearing you. Today: in your next conversation, try summarising the other person's view before giving yours.
Sharpen the saw

Imagine someone exhausted from sawing a tree who refuses to stop and sharpen the saw because they're too busy sawing. Covey's final habit is regular renewal of body, mind, relationships and spirit. Without maintenance, effectiveness wears down. Rest, exercise, learning and connection aren't luxuries; they're what make sustained effort possible. Today: choose one way to sharpen your saw, like a walk, a good book or a call with a friend, and do it.

books.title: Grit
books.author: Angela Duckworth
books.description: Research showing that passion and perseverance often matter more than talent.
ideas: Effort counts twice

Angela Duckworth's research suggests a simple but powerful formula: talent times effort equals skill, and skill times effort equals achievement. Effort counts twice. Talent matters, but without sustained effort it stays potential. Someone less talented who keeps working can overtake someone gifted who doesn't. Today: think of one skill you've been relying on talent for, and commit to a regular practice routine to develop it further.
Grit is passion plus perseverance

Grit, Duckworth explains, is a combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. Gritty people stick with their goals for years, through setbacks, boredom and plateaus. They don't necessarily work harder every day; they keep showing up over time. Grit can be developed. Today: identify one long-term goal you care about, and write down how you'll keep going when it gets boring or difficult.
Interest comes first

Passion rarely arrives fully formed. Duckworth found that it usually starts with a spark of interest, then deepens through practice, and later grows into a sense of purpose, a feeling that your work matters to others. Interest comes first and needs to be nurtured. Today: notice one small interest that's been calling you, and give it some time this week, without pressure to turn it into a passion yet.
Hope as a habit

Gritty people, Duckworth observes, tend to expect that their efforts will improve their future. That kind of hope isn't blind optimism; it's a habit of interpreting setbacks as temporary and fixable. When things go wrong, they ask what they can do differently rather than giving up. Today: think of a recent setback and write down one specific thing you could try next time.

books.title: Pro Git
books.author: Scott Chacon & Ben Straub
books.description: The standard guide to Git, the version-control system almost every software team uses.

free.note: Free online, plus PDF and EPUB downloads from the official site.

ideas: Snapshots, not differences

Many people imagine version control as a list of small changes. Git works differently: each commit is a snapshot of your whole project at that moment. To save space, files that haven't changed are simply reused from earlier snapshots. This design makes switching between versions and comparing them fast and reliable. Today: if you use Git, try browsing an old commit with your project's history view, and notice how easily you can see the project as it once was.
Three states

In Git, a file can be modified in your working folder, staged when you choose to include it in the next commit, and committed once it's saved permanently in history. The staging step lets you build clean, focused commits instead of saving every change at once. It's like packing a box deliberately rather than throwing everything in. Today: next time you commit, stage only the changes that belong together, and write a clear message describing them.
Branches are cheap

In some version control systems, branches are heavy and slow. In Git, a branch is just a lightweight pointer to a commit, so creating one costs almost nothing. That encourages experimenting: try an idea on its own branch, and merge it only if it works. Today: if you're about to try something risky in a project, create a new branch first, so your main work stays safe.
Everything is local

Almost every Git operation works on your own machine, using the full history stored locally. You can commit, compare and browse history without an internet connection, and it's fast because nothing travels over a network. Collaboration happens when you choose to push or pull. Today: if you're working somewhere with poor internet, remember that you can keep committing locally and sync later.
Rewrite only unpublished history

Git lets you rewrite history with tools like rebase, to clean up messy commits before sharing them. But rewriting history that other people already have causes painful conflicts. The rule of thumb is simple: tidy up your local work before you share it, and leave published history alone. Today: before pushing your changes, review your recent commits and tidy any messy messages, but only on work you haven't shared yet.

books.title: Think Python
books.author: Allen B. Downey
books.description: A friendly introduction to programming and computational thinking, using Python.

free.note: Free PDF and HTML from the publisher under a Creative Commons license.

ideas: Programming is problem solving

Learning to program isn't mainly about memorising syntax. Allen Downey emphasises that the core skill is problem solving: breaking a problem into small steps a computer can follow, then checking each step works. Programming teaches a way of thinking that's useful far beyond code. Today: take a small problem, even something like planning a trip, and break it into clear, simple steps as if you were writing instructions for a computer.
Debugging is experimentation

Debugging, Downey suggests, is like doing science. When a program misbehaves, form a hypothesis about what's wrong, change one thing, and observe what happens. Read error messages carefully; they often point near the real problem. Patience and curiosity beat frustration. Today: next time something doesn't work, in code or elsewhere, change only one thing at a time and observe the result before trying the next.
Functions tame complexity

Wrapping a few lines of code into a named function lets you reuse them, test them on their own and think about the program at a higher level. Instead of a long, tangled script, you get a set of clear building blocks. Downey shows how functions tame complexity. Today: if you write code, find one chunk you've repeated and turn it into a function with a descriptive name.
Incremental development

Downey recommends incremental development: write a little code, run it, check that it works, then add a little more. If something breaks, you know it was the last small change. Writing hundreds of lines before testing often leads to confusing errors that are hard to trace. Today: in your next project, of any kind, work in small steps and check each one before moving on.
